newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia confident of U.N. test ban vote.
newsitem.headline: Australia confident of U.N. test ban vote.

text.p: Australia said on Monday it was confident the United Nations would adopt its resolution for a nuclear test ban treaty, possibly as early as Tuesday, in a move which would bolster its candidature for a security council seat.

Australia's U.N. resolution on the Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty (CTBT) goes before the U.N. General Assembly later on Monday, with only India publicly opposing it, a foreign affairs department official said.

"India is the only country which has said it will not sign the CTBT," the official said in briefing reporters on an upcoming trip by Foreign Minister Alexander Downer to Europe, Britain and the United States.
"We now have confirmed co-sponsorship of 121 countries which is a good level." the official said. The general assembly totals 185 nations.
"The general assembly will start its consideration of the resolution today (Monday) New York time...and the actual vote might be as early as tomorrow (Tuesday)," she said.
The official said that if the resolution were adopted, the CTBT treaty could be signed on September 24.

After nearly three years of negotiations for a CTBT, India in August vetoed the draft treaty because it allows the five declared nuclear powers to refine their nuclear arsenals through laboratory tests. The draft also failed to commit them to a timetable for total disarmament.

India also said it opposed a clause that would require its signature to ratify the pact. New Delhi, which exploded a nuclear device in 1974 but has denied possessing atomic weapons, said the measure impinged on its sovereignty.
The five nuclear states are Britain, the United States, Russia, China and France, with India, Pakistan and Israel known as the three threshold states.
Australia said its recent strong endorsement of U.S. cruise missile attacks on Iraq, which lacked widespread support within the United Nations, would not harm its CTBT resolution.
Australia said a successful vote on the CTBT would in fact bolster its candidature for a U.N. Security Council seat, which it said was gaining support.

"We think it (the CTBT resolution) is very positive because it underlines the sort of role Australia plays in the international community and in particular the international security agenda," said another foreign affairs official.
"I think it can only be a positive for the (security council) campaign," he said.
The U.N. Security Council has five permanent seats, taken by the United States, Britain, Russia, France, China, and 10 non-permanent seats, which are held for two years.

Australia, which has held a security council seat four times, is competing against Portugal and Sweden for two of the temporary seats. The successful candidate requires a two-thirds vote of the general assembly.
"We feel we are in that vicinity...," said the official, adding that foreign minister Downer would visit New York between September 24 and October 4 for final lobbying.
A vote is expected at the end of October.
